sections.title_en: The Mitzva of Kiddush Hashem and the Prohibition of Ḥillul Hashem
sections.body_en:
Every Jew is commanded to sanctify the great and awesome Name and to refrain from desecrating it. Generally, Kiddush Hashem (sanctification of God's Name) is fulfilled by revealing faith and morality in ordinary life: by walking in the ways of God, doing righteousness and justice, being careful to avoid transgressions, and fulfilling mitzvot with devotion and joy. But sometimes, in difficult and terrible times, when a Jew is pressed by wicked people to betray the faith of Israel and to commit a severe transgression that entails Ḥillul Hashem (desecration of God's Name), the mitzva of Kiddush Hashem obliges him to give up his life for the sanctity of God's Name and not to commit that severe and unbearable transgression. As it is stated (Vayikra 22:31-33): "You shall keep My commandments and do them; I am the Lord. You shall not profane My holy Name, and I shall be sanctified in the midst of the Children of Israel; I am the Lord who sanctifies you, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God; I am the Lord." The Sages said (Sifra ibid.): "On a condition I brought you out of the land of Egypt: on condition that you give yourselves over to sanctify My Name…".

The role of Israel is to reveal and publicise the faith in God's unity, and thereby to draw life and blessing into the world. The existence of the world, its perfection and its redemption depend on this. This great destiny should fill every Jew with tremendous love for God, so that he will always walk in God's ways, and when required to do so, will even give up his life for the sanctity of His Name, blessed be He, the source of his life and his soul. As it is stated (Devarim 6:4-5): "Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might." "'With all your soul' – even if He takes your soul" (Mishna Berakhot 9:5). Therefore, although the mitzvot of the Torah were given so that we might live by them, and for this reason saving life (pikuaḥ nefesh) overrides the mitzvot, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:5): "You shall keep My statutes and My laws, which a person shall do and live by them" – "'and live by them' – and not die by them" (Yoma 85b) – when it comes to Kiddush Hashem and preventing its desecration at the most severe level, one must be killed rather than transgress (yehareg ve-al ya'avor). There are three levels of this:

1) When a Jew is coerced to commit one of the three severe transgressions – idolatry, forbidden sexual relations (gilui arayot) and bloodshed – he must be killed rather than transgress.

2) For the other transgressions in the Torah, if the coercion is meant to make him transgress his religion in public (be-farhesya) – he must be killed rather than transgress. But if the coercion is for the personal pleasure of the coercer, or to make him transgress his religion but not in public, that is, not in the presence of ten Jews – he should transgress and not be killed.

3) In a time of persecution (she'at ha-shemad), that is, when a decree is issued against Israel to make them abandon their religion, even in private – he must be killed rather than transgress any of the Torah's mitzvot.

Another supreme level of Kiddush Hashem is that of IDF soldiers who go out to battle in defence of the people and the land. So great is this mitzva that it is the only one that obliges a Jew to risk his life. For all the mitzvot for which one must be killed rather than transgress, if he is able to flee, he should flee and be saved; but one may not evade going out to battle (see Peninei Halakha, Ha-am Ve-ha-aretz 4:1-4).1

notes_en.en: The mitzva of Kiddush Hashem is fulfilled in all of a person's conduct, even in private, but even more so in public, as the Sages said (Sota 10b): "Yosef, who sanctified the Name of Heaven in private, merited that one letter of the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, was added to his name; Yehuda, who sanctified the Name of Heaven in public, merited that his entire name is called by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He." Rambam wrote likewise (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:10-11). The basis of the obligation of mesirut nefesh (self-sacrifice) lies in the mitzva of "and I shall be sanctified," that is, in the mitzva to sanctify the Name of Heaven and to refrain from desecrating God's Name, as Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:1-2; Sefer Ha-mitzvot, positive commandment 9, negative commandment 63). However, some Rishonim explained that the obligation to be killed rather than transgress in private in the case of the three severe transgressions, even though there is apparently no Ḥillul Hashem in this, stems from the severity of these transgressions; so wrote Ramban and Nimukei Yosef. Yet even from their own words it emerges that the obligation of self-sacrifice for the three transgressions is rooted in love of God and the sanctification of His Name, similar to self-sacrifice in a time of persecution (see Ramban, Shemot 20:6). The reason one must be killed rather than commit them even when the coercion is in private and for the gentile's pleasure is that one who commits them grievously harms the Divine image within him, and thereby desecrates the Name of Heaven even when this is not apparent to others. Moreover, even in private there is at least one gentile present who sees the Jew committing severe transgressions, and this too is Ḥillul Hashem (Avnei Nezer YD 128:4-5; Rav Goren, Torat Ha-shabbat Ve-ha-mo'ed, p. 388). For their abizraihu as well, that is, the derivatives of these transgressions, one must be killed rather than transgress, because of the great Ḥillul Hashem in these transgressions (below, section 4, and notes 15 and 19; Sefat Emet, Pesaḥim 25a; Ḥavat Binyamin 93). In summary, the mitzva of Kiddush Hashem is a general mitzva that branches out into levels: for the three severe transgressions one must always be killed rather than transgress; for other transgressions, only when they involve public Ḥillul Hashem by making one transgress his religion, and in a time of persecution even in private. The mitzva of Kiddush Hashem further branches out into all of a person's conduct: the more righteously he behaves, the more he sanctifies the Name of Heaven, and the more wickedly he acts, the more he desecrates the Name of Heaven (Yad Peshuta, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah, introduction to chapter 5).

sections.title_en: The Exalted Status of Those Who Sanctify God's Name
sections.body_en:
Those who give up their lives for Kiddush Hashem attain the most exalted level, above which there is none. In dying for Kiddush Hashem they rise above the individual framework in which every person dwells to the collective level of the holiness of Israel, and they become bound to God and sanctified with His holiness. Therefore, although they die with their days cut short in this world, they live intensely in the world that is entirely long – in the World to Come – to the point that "no creature can stand within their partition" (Bava Batra 10b). In their merit, life in this world continues and grows stronger, for out of their lives in this world they merited to be sanctified with supernal holiness, and thereby revealed the highest point of holiness in this world. The foundation of the holiness of self-sacrifice is the Binding of Yitzḥak (Akedat Yitzḥak), which expresses the unique quality (segula) of Israel. Therefore, when the shofar is blown on Rosh Ha-shana, together with the remembrance of the Binding of Yitzḥak, all the holy ones who gave up their lives for the sanctity of God's Name rise up and are remembered (Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 4:15).

By the way of nature, human societies tend to sink into the routine of the present and to forget the great vision of the redemption of the world. This situation leads to crises, since the soul always yearns for more, and when it finds no positive channel for its longings, the yearning bursts out in evil ways that lead society to wickedness and ruin. The righteous, who cleave to the values of truth and goodness that sustain the world, are forced to face difficult and terrible trials. And when they withstand the trial and give up their lives for Kiddush Hashem, they connect the life of the present to eternal values and remind Israel of the great vision, and in that merit the world endures and advances toward its redemption. Of them it is stated (Tehillim 50:5): "Gather to Me My pious ones, those who made a covenant with Me over sacrifice." The Sages said (Sanhedrin 110b): "'Gather to Me My pious ones' – these are the righteous of every generation; 'those who made a covenant with Me' – these are Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya, who gave themselves over into the fiery furnace; 'over sacrifice' – these are Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, who gave themselves over to slaughter for the words of Torah." It is fitting in our day to continue expounding the verse "And the heavens declared His righteousness" – these are the soldiers and settlers who risked their lives in defence of the people and the land.

The holy ones express love of God at the highest level, as the Sages said (Shir Ha-shirim Rabba 8:4): "'For love is strong as death' – the love with which the generation of persecution loved the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is stated (Tehillim 44:23): 'For Your sake we are killed all day long; we are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.'"

The Sages said (Shoḥer Tov, Tehillim 16:4) that although the suffering of those killed for the sanctification of His Name is great, the Holy One, blessed be He, said that they have lost nothing, and their blood is more precious before Him than all the sacrifices. They are the foundation of the world's existence, for they express the absolute bond of the creatures to the source of their life. As the Sages said (Bereishit Rabba 34:9), when the scent of those who sanctify God's Name rose up from Noaḥ's offering, God swore that He would no longer curse the ground. For as long as there are people in the world prepared to give themselves up for the sanctity of God's Name, even though the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth, the bond to the source of life is stronger and the world endures. As it is stated: "'For He founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers' – in what merit? In the merit of 'the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face (those who sanctify God's Name), Ya'akov, Selah'" (Tehillim 24:2, 6). It emerges that their self-sacrifice is like the Tamid offering, which expresses the absolute bond of Israel to the source of their life (see Menaḥot 110b, and Tosafot there, s.v. "Mikha'el"; Peninei Halakha, Tefila 13:2, 5).

The Sages said (Sifra, Aḥarei Mot 8:13) that God said to Israel: "If you sanctify My Name, I too will sanctify My Name through you" – to bring redemption to the world. So great is the Kiddush Hashem brought about through those who give up their lives that, as it were, already at the moment they are killed, the vengeance that God will in the future take upon the wicked who killed them is fixed and accomplished, and already now they are as if about to rise at the Resurrection of the Dead; and God says at that moment: "Today I am exalted through them before the eyes of the nations of the world who deny the Torah; today I exact retribution for them from their enemies; today I resurrect the dead through them. I am the Lord – I am a Judge to exact retribution and faithful to pay reward."

Jews who did not intend to give up their lives and were killed only because they were Jews, such as those killed in the Holocaust or in acts of terror against the Jewish people, are also considered holy. For over the long course of history it has become clear to all that Israel expresses the faith in God's unity, and by the very fact of identifying as Jews they bear God's Name, and the wicked of the world wish to kill them. Therefore, the very act of identifying as a Jew contains a readiness for self-sacrifice, and anyone killed for being a Jew is considered like a soldier who fell for Kiddush Hashem in the heroic war for the survival of the Jewish people.

The Sages said that the Holy One, blessed be He, will avenge the blood of those who gave up their lives for Kiddush Hashem, as it is stated (Tehillim 110:6): "He will judge among the nations, filling [the land] with corpses; He will crush the head over a great land." When Israel is worthy, the vengeance comes through the soldiers of Israel; when they are not worthy, the vengeance is delayed and comes in indirect ways. The Sages further said that in the upper worlds there is one appointed over all the Jews killed by the gentiles, and he records their names on the garment of the Holy One, blessed be He; they will remain recorded there until God avenges their blood, and until the Mashiaḥ is revealed and comes to comfort them, and with him lights and delights will descend to gladden them, and angels will clothe them in garments of glory (Zohar I 39a; 41a).2

notes_en.en:
Although there are levels in the readiness to give up one's life and be sanctified, even one who was killed by the enemies of Israel because of his Jewish identity is called 'kadosh' (holy), since he was killed for being a member of God's people. This also emerges from the Zohar cited above. It is likewise implied by Ḥatam Sofer (YD 333), who called one killed by a gentile 'kadosh'. The same applies to an apostate. True, as a rule one does not mourn for an apostate, as explained in SA YD 345:5: "All who separate from the ways of the community – these are people who have cast off the yoke of the mitzvot from their necks and are not included in the community of Israel in their conduct, in honouring the festivals, and in attending synagogues and study halls, but rather are like free men unto themselves, like the other nations – and likewise apostates and informers: for all of these one does not observe aninut and does not mourn." However, Rema wrote (YD 340:5): "Some say that an apostate who was killed by an idolater is mourned." (Shakh 10 explained that since he was killed unjustly, this brings him atonement; and Levush wrote that presumably he had thoughts of repentance.) Likewise, Maran Ha-rav Kook explained (Ma'amarei Ha-re'iya, pp. 93, 460) that those killed for being Jews are called holy.
A higher level is that of a soldier or settler who is prepared to put himself at risk for the defence of the people and the settlement of the Land, and is killed in the course of his mitzva, for he knew that the mitzva involved a certain risk and nevertheless devoted himself to performing it. Above them is the level of soldiers who go out to battle in wartime and risk their lives in defence of the people and the Land; their level is like that of those who give up their lives so as not to transgress their religion. See Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 4:12.

sections.body_en:
One who is coerced to worship idolatry under threat to his life is commanded to sanctify God's Name and to be killed rather than worship, as it is stated (Vayikra 22:32): "You shall not profane My holy Name, and I shall be sanctified in the midst of the Children of Israel; I am the Lord who sanctifies you." And it is stated (Devarim 6:5): "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might"; the Sages said (Mishna Berakhot 9:5): "'With all your soul' – even if He takes your soul." "Rabbi Eliezer says: If it is stated 'with all your soul,' why is it stated 'with all your might'? And if it is stated 'with all your might,' why is it stated 'with all your soul'? If you have a person whose body is dearer to him than his money, for him it is stated 'with all your soul'; and if you have a person whose money is dearer to him than his body, for him it is stated 'with all your might'" (Sanhedrin 74a).

The same law applies to bloodshed: if a person is coerced to kill his fellow under threat that if he does not do so they will kill him – he must be killed rather than kill. For it is inconceivable that a person should save himself by murdering his fellow – is his blood redder than his fellow's blood?! Moreover, the very permission to transgress the mitzvot of the Torah for the sake of saving life is learned from the verse "and live by them," and is meant to add life, not that a person should murder his fellow in order to save himself.

The law of forbidden sexual relations is like the law of bloodshed, as it is stated (Devarim 22:26): "For as when a man rises against his fellow and murders him, so is this matter." Therefore, if a person is coerced to have relations with a woman forbidden to him under the prohibitions of arayot, under threat that if he does not do so they will kill him – he must be killed rather than transgress (Sanhedrin 74a; Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:2; SA YD 157:1).

Although for all three severe transgressions one must be killed rather than transgress, there is a certain difference between them in the reason for their severity. With idolatry, the severity of the transgression lies in the betrayal of the faith in God's unity and of the vision of perfecting the world, whereas with bloodshed and forbidden relations the main severity of the transgression lies in the grievous harm to the other person, to the Divine image within him.

As an extension of the mitzva of self-sacrifice for the faith in God's unity and of the prohibition of idolatry, when a person is coerced in public to transgress one of the Torah's mitzvot in order to show that he is betraying God, it is no longer a matter of a single mitzva but of faith in God as a whole, and therefore he must give up his life as for idolatry. We will first explain the law of coercion to commit idolatry and all the other mitzvot, and afterwards (below, sections 17-20) the laws of coercion to commit bloodshed and forbidden relations.

If a Jew was coerced to worship idolatry, for example to bow down to an idol or to offer a sacrifice before it, even if he was coerced to do so in private, he must be killed rather than transgress, as it is stated: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul" – even if He takes your soul (Mishna Berakhot 9:5; Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:2; SA YD 157:1). For everything forbidden because of idolatry one must "be killed rather than transgress," including acts that express honour or love for the idol, such as hugging and kissing the idol (above, 3:3).

Even a person who is dangerously ill is forbidden to be healed by a remedy believed to depend on the power of idolatry, for example by a special incantation belonging to it, lest following the remedy's success people be drawn to worship that idolatry. The Sages said: "It happened that Ben Dama, the son of Rabbi Yishmael's sister, was bitten by a snake, and Ya'akov of Kfar Sekhanya came to heal him, but Rabbi Yishmael did not allow him." For this Ya'akov would heal with an incantation invoking the name of the Nazarene. "He (Ben Dama) said to him: Rabbi Yishmael, my brother, let him be, so that I may be healed by him, and I will bring a verse from the Torah showing that it is permitted. He had not finished speaking before his soul departed and he died. Rabbi Yishmael proclaimed over him: Fortunate are you, Ben Dama, for your body is pure and your soul departed in purity, and you did not transgress the words of your colleagues." The Sages explained that Ben Dama wished to argue that it is permitted to be healed through faith in the Nazarene, since saving life overrides the prohibition. However, the halakha is that this is forbidden, because healing by the power of faith in idolatry expresses faith in idolatry (Avoda Zara 27b; Tosafot s.v. "Shani"; SA 155:1).

Similarly, if an idolatrous physician said that a dangerously ill patient's cure lies in the water of a certain idolatry, or in the leaves of an Ashera tree, even though the patient is in danger and about to die, it is forbidden to be healed by them, for one may not be healed through idolatry. But if the physician said that he needs water from a certain place or from a certain tree, without mentioning that they belong to idolatry, it is permitted. For it is possible that it is the nature of this water or these leaves that heals, and not their belonging to idolatry (Pesaḥim 25a; Tosafot and Rosh, Avoda Zara 27b). Some are stringent in this case too, because of the Torah prohibition against deriving benefit from anything belonging to idolatry (Ran), but the halakha follows the lenient opinion that one must be killed only for an act that expresses faith in idolatry (SA 155:2; Shakh 11).3

notes_en.en:
In Pesaḥim 25a it is cited in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan that even in a case of danger to life one may not be healed with the wood of an Ashera; and in Avoda Zara 27b it is cited that even in a case of danger to life one may not be healed with an incantation of idolatry. From here the Rishonim learned that one must be killed rather than transgress even for the abizraihu (ancillary prohibitions) of idolatry, that is, even for prohibitions that are not actual idolatry but branch out from it. According to most Rishonim, only when the cure is attributed to the power of the idolatry is there an expression of faith in idolatry and a concern that people will be drawn after it, and therefore one must be killed rather than transgress; this is why Rabbi Yishmael was stringent not to be healed by the incantation of the Nazarene, as explained in Yerushalmi Avoda Zara 2:2. So wrote Tosafot (Avoda Zara 27b, s.v. "Shani"), Semag, Roke'aḥ, Teruma, Rashba, Rosh, Ritva and Tur. Some hold that even when there is no concern that people will be drawn to believe in it, one must be killed rather than transgress the prohibitions that branch out from idolatry, including the prohibition of being healed with the leaves of an Ashera, since it is forbidden by Torah law to derive benefit from them, as it is stated (Devarim 13:18): "And nothing of the banned property shall cling to your hand." So wrote Ramban and Ran. And according to Rivash one must be stringent even regarding a rabbinic prohibition of benefit. According to many, those who are stringent even without an expression of faith in idolatry are stringent only regarding a Torah prohibition, and in their view this is also the opinion of Rema (Shakh 157:10; Gra 14; see Shevet Yehuda YD 150:2, who summarised the discussion). SA 155:2 cites the stringent opinion as "some say," and the lenient opinion as the unattributed opinion, which is the main opinion. So too hold most Aḥaronim: the halakha follows most Rishonim, that only when the act contains an expression of faith in idolatry must one be killed rather than transgress (Levush; Shakh 155:11; Shiyarei Knesset Ha-gedola; Ḥokhmat Adam; and others).
According to many, although hugging and kissing an idol are not among the forms of worship punishable by death, since they are forbidden by Torah law (above, 3:3), their law is like the abizraihu of idolatry, for which one must be killed rather than transgress. This is certainly the opinion of Ramban and Ran, and according to most Aḥaronim it is also the opinion of Tosafot and those who agree with them (Ḥatam Sofer 2:133; Minḥat Ḥinukh 296:15).
Some say that even a person coerced to make an idol for others must be killed rather than transgress (Rav Tzadok of Lublin in Otzar Ha-melekh, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4). But according to many, since he is not worshipping idolatry, and the idol has not yet been worshipped and therefore is not yet forbidden for benefit, and there is only a negative commandment here, according to all opinions he should transgress and not be killed (Re'em, Shemot 32:21; Maharik 250; Parashat Ha-kesef, Avoda Zara 3:9; and others. See Minḥat Ḥinukh 27:8).
The Sages forbade drinking from the mouth of an idol, because of mar'it ayin (how it appears to onlookers), since it looks as if one is kissing it (Avoda Zara 12a). Some say that even if he would die of thirst he must not drink (Rashba). But according to many, in a case of danger he may drink from the idol (Ran; Rema 150:3; and many Aḥaronim), and this is what I wrote as the halakha (below, 12:3, note 2).

sections.title_en: Other Transgressions in Ordinary Times and in a Time of Persecution
sections.body_en:
If a Jew was coerced to transgress one of the Torah's mitzvot for the coercer's personal benefit, for example, a gentile ordered him on Shabbat to harvest his field or to cook his food, then even when the desecration of Shabbat is done in public – he should transgress and not be killed. And if it is not in public, even if the gentile has no benefit from it and his entire intention is to make him transgress his religion, for example, he ordered the Jew to kindle a fire on Shabbat without gaining anything from it – he should transgress and not be killed, since there is no public Ḥillul Hashem in this. But if the aim of the coercion is to make him transgress his religion in public, in order to show everyone that he is betraying his faith, for example, he coerced him in front of many people to light a fire on Shabbat without any benefit – he must be killed rather than transgress. And even if the coercion concerns a minor mitzva – he must be killed rather than transgress (Sanhedrin 74b; Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:2; SA 157:1).

The Sages gave an example of a minor mitzva: 'arketa de-mesana', that is, the shoelace. Jews were accustomed to lace their shoes in a particular way, and when the coercion regarding this was in public, in order to show everyone that the Jew was transgressing his religion – he must be killed rather than transgress. Some say this is on condition that changing the lacing involves a Torah prohibition, such as the prohibition "nor shall you walk in their statutes" (Vayikra 18:3), which forbids wearing something that expresses faith in idolatry or that violates the rules of modesty (Beit Yosef according to Rif and Rambam). Others say that even when the lacing is merely a distinctively Jewish custom, he must be killed rather than change it, for if he changes it he will appear to be betraying his religion (Rashi and Yere'im).

In a time of persecution, when the enemies of Israel wish to make Israel abandon their religion, or a single mitzva out of all the mitzvot, then even when the coercion is in private, in order to make him transgress his religion – he must be killed rather than transgress. For in a time of persecution one must strengthen oneself all the more in loyalty to the Torah and the mitzvot and beware of Ḥillul Hashem. Moreover, if a Jew yields to them even in private, his surrender will encourage them to continue coercing Israel to transgress their religion (Rashi, Ran).4

notes_en.en:
Sanhedrin 74a: "Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: They voted and concluded in the upper story of the house of Nitza in Lod: For all the transgressions in the Torah, if a person is told, 'Transgress and you will not be killed,' he should transgress and not be killed, except for idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed." 'They voted and concluded' – meaning that they decided that for the three severe transgressions one must be killed rather than transgress even in private, unlike the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael (below, at the end of the note). Regarding other transgressions, addressing both ordinary times and a time of persecution, they said in Sanhedrin 74a-b: "When Rav Dimi came, he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: … In a time of persecution, even for a minor mitzva one must be killed rather than transgress. When Ravin came, he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Even not in a time of persecution, they said this only in private, but in public, even for a minor mitzva one must be killed rather than transgress. What is a minor mitzva? Rava bar Yitzḥak said in the name of Rav: Even to change a shoe strap (arketa de-mesana)" (as explained below).
According to the main opinion, which is that of most Rishonim and Aḥaronim, for the three severe transgressions one must be killed rather than transgress in every case, even in private and for the gentile's own pleasure. For all other transgressions, including arketa de-mesana: in public, in order to make one transgress his religion – he must be killed rather than transgress; not in public, or not with the aim of making him transgress his religion – he should transgress and not be killed. And in a time of persecution, when the aim is to make him transgress his religion, even in private – he must be killed rather than transgress. This is the opinion of Rambam (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:1-4); Ra'avan, Semag, Nimukei Yosef, Yad Ramah, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Ran, Tur and SA 157:1; Taz 3; Shakh 7; and many others. This is also implied by Rashi, Ramban and Ritva. (At the end of the note we will cite two approaches that departed from the main opinion toward stringency and one approach that departed toward leniency.)
The definition of 'making one transgress his religion': According to the main approach, only when the sole intention of the coercers is to make him transgress his religion is the coercion considered 'to make him transgress his religion'; but if an intention of personal benefit for the gentile was also joined to it, it is no longer considered coercion against religion. As Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:2): "If he intended only to make him transgress the mitzvot … in the presence of ten Jews – he must be killed rather than transgress" (Yad Peshuta). Maran Ha-rav Kook distinguished between a government decree aimed at making people transgress their religion – where even if personal benefit is joined to it, one must be killed rather than transgress – and coercion by a private individual, where if personal benefit is joined to it, one should transgress and not be killed (Mishpat Kohen 148, p. 354).
A minor mitzva, such as arketa de-mesana (a shoe strap): Some say this refers to the Torah prohibition of following the statutes of the gentiles (Yad Ramah, Ra'ah, Beit Yosef according to Rif and Rambam; and many understood the Rosh this way). Others say that a rabbinic mitzva is also included (Ritva; Rambam, as is clear from Iggeret Ha-shemad, and as explained in Pri Ḥadash and Yad Peshuta). Still others say that even a Jewish custom is included, and it seems their intention is a distinctively Jewish custom whose change looks like uprooting a mitzva (Rav Sherira Gaon, Rashi, Rabbi Yehonatan of Lunel, Riaz, Yere'im 403). 'Shemad' applies even to one mitzva out of all the mitzvot, as explained in Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:3 (but it seems this is on condition that the intention is to make them abandon the entire Torah; below, note 7). When the decree of persecution is not only against Jews, for example they decreed that Jews and Muslims must eat pork, according to Nimukei Yosef this is not a time of persecution; so wrote Beit Yosef and Rema 157:1, and Shakh 6. According to Ra'avad this too is a time of persecution (and many explained Rambam this way). According to Maran Ha-rav Kook (Mishpat Kohen 148, p. 356), only when the decree is for the benefit of the government, for example in order to unify its subjects – then, if it also applies to gentiles, it is not considered a time of persecution.
Additional approaches: Having learned the main opinion, we will mention two approaches that departed from the main opinion toward stringency and one approach that departed toward leniency. Those stringent regarding other transgressions: According to Semak, Mordekhai and Orḥot Ḥayim, for other transgressions, only when the coercion is to commit a transgression in private for the gentile's benefit should one transgress and not be killed. But if the coercion is in public for the coercer's own benefit, or in private in order to make him transgress his religion – he must be killed rather than transgress.
Those stringent in a time of persecution: According to Ra'avad, Ra'ah and Ohel Mo'ed, in a time of persecution, even when the coercion is for the coercer's benefit and in private – he must be killed and not transgress. (According to Baḥ and Or Gadol, this is also the opinion of Rambam and others. Apparently they had not seen Rambam's Iggeret Ha-shemad, in which he wrote that even in a time of persecution, if the intention is not to make one transgress his religion, he should transgress and not be killed. And as a practical ruling [?], according to Rambam, in a time of persecution, in public, one should be stringent even when it is for the coercers' own benefit.)
The opinion of Rabbi Yishmael: Rabbi Yishmael agrees that for other transgressions, in public in order to make one transgress his religion – he must be killed rather than transgress (Rosh, Avoda Zara 2:9; Rashba, Avoda Zara 27b; and others). He also agrees that in a time of persecution one must be killed rather than commit any transgression, even in private (Ritva and Meiri, Avoda Zara 54a). But there is disagreement regarding his view of the three severe transgressions. Some say he is lenient regarding coercion to worship idolatry in private for the coercers' own benefit, so that one should transgress and not be killed; but for forbidden relations and bloodshed one must be killed rather than transgress (Rabbeinu Elḥanan, Avoda Zara 27b; Minḥat Ḥinukh 295:1). According to Razah and Meiri, he is also lenient regarding forbidden relations if the coercion is in private and for the coercers' own benefit, and only for bloodshed must one be killed rather than transgress (although according to Razah, as a rule, coercion to commit idolatry is for the purpose of coercion against religion). Others say that according to Rabbi Yishmael, even for bloodshed in private one should transgress and not be killed; so wrote Tosafot and Tosafot Rabbeinu Shimshon of Sens, Ketubot 19a; Rosh, Avoda Zara 2:9. It seems their words refer to a case where the person they want killed will be killed in any event, so that the reasoning of 'what makes you think [your blood is redder]' does not apply, for example, when they demand that one person be handed over to death, and if not they will kill everyone. So wrote Rav Gershuni in Ḥokhmat Gershon, p. 319, and Rav Yisraeli in Ḥavat Binyamin 93.
Those lenient following Rabbi Yishmael: Some say that according to Rava (Ketubot 19a) the halakha follows Rabbi Yishmael, and therefore in private, for idolatry and forbidden relations, one should transgress and not be killed, and only for bloodshed must one be killed rather than transgress (Piskei Rid, Pesaḥim 25b). Others say that even for bloodshed in private (as explained in the previous paragraph) one should transgress and not be killed; so ruled in practice Hagahot Asheri in the name of Ri, Ketubot 19a.

sections.body_en:
Coercion to commit a transgression in public in order to make a Jew transgress his religion means coercion in the presence of at least ten Jews, for so the Sages expounded from the verse (Vayikra 22:32): "and I shall be sanctified in the midst of the Children of Israel" (Sanhedrin 74b; Megilla 23b). The existence and perfection of the world depend on Israel's being loyal to the Torah with all their heart and all their soul, and through this the faith and Torah of Israel will gradually be revealed throughout the world. Therefore, when a Jew yields and gives up his faith in the presence of ten Jews, an especially great Ḥillul Hashem is caused, and he must be killed rather than transgress. But if there were not ten Jews present, even if there were many gentiles there, he should transgress and not be killed.

Even when there are not ten Jews who actually see the transgression being committed, if the matter is known to many, it is considered public.5

Many have written that a person who must give up his life for Kiddush Hashem, in addition to saying 'Shema Yisrael' as Rabbi Akiva did (below, section 12), should recite the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to sanctify His Name." And if he is in the presence of ten: "to sanctify His Name in public" (Recanati; Responsa Maharshal 64; Ya'avetz; Pitḥei Teshuva 157:6. According to the Shela, he should recite the blessing only when the self-sacrifice is in public).

notes_en.en:
From the Gemara's question in Sanhedrin 74b – why did Esther not give up her life when she was taken to Aḥashverosh, since this was in public? – we learn that although people did not see her having relations with Aḥashverosh, since the matter was known to all, it is considered public (Ran, Meiri, Ritva, Radbaz, Maharik; Shakh 157:4; unlike Binyan Tziyon 1:64. For the answer to the question, see below, note 9). However, one must say that since those who know of the transgression are not present before us, there must be certainty that at least ten people know of it at the time of the act, so that presumably, because of the doubt, many more than ten would be required. And some wrote explicitly that when the publicity is only through knowledge and not through seeing, it must be "known to all" (Tashbetz 1:158), "revealed and publicised to all" (Maharik 137).
The Sages' exposition that ten constitute a public was learned from the congregation of Koraḥ and from the spies (Sanhedrin 74b); hence Ḥillul Hashem in public applies even in the presence of ten apostates (Igrot Moshe YD 1:70). It is doubtful whether the person being killed counts toward the ten (Devar Shmuel 63; Pitḥei Teshuva 157:7). According to Minḥat Ḥinukh (296:10), women do not count toward the quorum of ten, as with the minyan for devarim she-bi-kedusha (matters of holiness). On the other hand, some say that they do count, since women, like men, are obligated in the mitzva of Kiddush Hashem and self-sacrifice (Or Gadol, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:1; Einayim La-mishpat, Sanhedrin 74a. See Peninei Halakha, Tefila 2, note 1; the matter requires further study).

sections.body_en:
When a Jew is required to declare that he accepts another religion, even if he is not required at that time to perform any act, and the acceptance of the religion takes place in private before the coercing ruler, and that religion does not involve idol worship, such as Islam – he must be killed rather than convert. For one who believes in another religion denies the Torah of Moshe and thereby desecrates the Name of Heaven, and as a result will also come to commit many severe transgressions (Ritva, Pesaḥim 25b; Radbaz 4:92). This trial was very difficult, and throughout the terrible exile, when darkness covered the earth, many Jews were pressed by Muslims or Christians to convert. To our sorrow, many did not withstand the terrible trial and converted, but very many gave up their lives for the sanctity of God's Name and did not convert, and in their merit the Jewish people lives and endures (see Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it Ve-yovel 11, note 3).

The obligation to give up one's life rather than declare a conversion applies on condition that the declaration truly expresses a change of religion. But when it expresses respect and acceptance of authority without a commitment to convert – he should transgress and not be killed. As Rambam wrote in Iggeret Ha-shemad: when Muslims coerce a Jew to declare that he believes in their prophet, but do not coerce him actually to transgress any of the Torah's mitzvot, and he can observe them in secret, and everyone knows that his declaration is meant to show respect for their religion and not out of belief – he should make the declaration and not be killed. True, if he sanctified God's Name and was killed, he has a reward for this; but initially, it is proper that he make the declaration and not be killed, and afterwards strive with all his ability to move quickly to a land where he can serve God without any coercion (Yad Peshuta, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4).6

notes_en.en: Rosh wrote (Avoda Zara 2:4) that even when a Jew is threatened with death, he is forbidden to say that he is an idolater or a gentile. So wrote Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Tur 157:2 and Radbaz. It seems that Rosh's intention refers to a situation in which a Jew is required to say that he is converting to Christianity, for then he would no longer be able to retract, since by law in the Christian kingdoms one who retracted his conversion faced the death penalty. These are the words of the Rosh: "Since they want to kill him if he does not convert to their religion and become an idolater like them, certainly when he says he is an idolater, he has acknowledged their religion and accepted their god upon himself." So wrote Responsa Mi-ma'amakim 5:3. Even one who does not agree with this interpretation of the Rosh will agree that if he can save himself by saying something that can be understood in two ways, and the gentile will err and understand from it that he is a gentile or a believer in their religion, he should do so in order to be saved from the danger (Nedarim 62b; Terumat Ha-deshen 196; Rema 157:2).

sections.body_en:
As we learned (in section 5), in a time of persecution, when a Jew is ordered to change his clothing to that of a gentile in order to make him transgress his religion – even in private, he must be killed rather than transgress. However, all this applies when he is coerced to wear gentile clothing in order to make him transgress his religion, and he obeys them. But if he wishes to flee from there, he may disguise himself as a gentile for that purpose. He may even wear a garment of sha'atnez (a forbidden wool-and-linen mixture) so that they will not suspect him of being a Jew. For as long as it is not known that he is a Jew, there is no Ḥillul Hashem in this, but only the violation of one of the Torah's mitzvot, and saving life overrides the prohibitions of the Torah (Nimukei Yosef, Bava Kamma 40b; Maharik 88; Radbaz 4:65; Shakh 157:17).

Likewise, the Midrash relates (Bereishit Rabba 82:8) that two students of Rabbi Yehoshua changed their clothing in a time of persecution in order to look like gentiles. An apostate officer recognised them and said to them: If you are loyal to the Torah, give up your lives for it and do not disguise yourselves! And if you are not loyal to the Torah, why, when you are forced to transgress its mitzvot, do you give up your lives for it? They said to him: We are loyal to the Torah, and for it we give up our lives, "but it is not the way of a person to destroy himself knowingly"; therefore, from the outset we try to escape the decree.

Similarly, Jewish merchants who needed to travel through places dangerous for Jews were accustomed to dress as gentiles so that they would not be harmed. However, it was only for a great need of livelihood that they permitted disguising oneself as a gentile, and without a great need it is forbidden (Baḥ; Shakh 157:19). But to downplay Jewish markers in order to prevent harassment is permitted even without a great need of livelihood, as long as one does not actually disguise oneself as a gentile; for example, wearing a hat instead of a kippa in order to conceal one's Jewishness.7

notes_en.en:
In 5604 (1844), the Russian government decreed that the Jews of Poland under its rule must change their clothing and shave their beards and pe'ot. According to Rav Shlomo Kluger (Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at 1:188), the government's intention was to make the Jews transgress their religion, and therefore they must be killed rather than transgress. So too held the Ḥiddushei Ha-Rim of Gur (Me'ir Einei Ha-gola, sections 404-407). However, his teacher, the Rebbe of Kotzk, held that they need not be killed, since clothing does not express Judaism (Beit Kotzk, p. 67). And according to the Rebbe of Kobrin (Imrot Moshe, Igrot Kodesh 1), since they did not decree that Jews must dress exactly like gentiles, one should not be killed. In addition, since there were Jews there who had changed their clothing of their own accord, if those who had not changed their clothing were to give up their lives over this, the Jews who had changed would think that they had left the community of Israel. End of quote. So too ruled Tzemaḥ Tzedek (YD 90), adding another reason: by not wearing Jewish clothing one transgresses passively (shev ve-al ta'aseh), and one is not killed for a passive transgression (below, section 9). Beit Shlomo (YD 197) wrote that one who had not changed his clothing and came to a place where they had decreed a change, and the Jews there had changed, may change while he is there. (It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that what the Sages said – that even when the decree concerns a single matter, if the intention is to make one transgress his religion, he must be killed rather than transgress, as explained in section 5 – applies on condition that the aim is to make him abandon the entire religion completely, as emerges from Rashi, Sanhedrin 74a, regarding private coercion in a time of persecution: if he yields in one matter, they will continue to coerce him in the other matters. But when it is known that the decree concerns only clothing, as long as changing one's clothing does not involve a Torah prohibition, he should transgress and not be killed.)
In the Holocaust, Jews were sometimes able to save themselves by saying that they were Christians. And although we learned that a Jew is forbidden to say that he is a Christian, the prohibition applies when his statement expressed submission to the gentiles' wish that he convert to their religion; but when the aim of the gentiles is to kill the seed of Israel even if they convert, this is not conversion but rescue in wartime, and therefore it is permitted and a mitzva. Rav Yeḥezkel Yaakobson wrote along these lines (Ha-ma'ayan, Tevet 5771). And Rav Herzog (Heikhal Yitzḥak, part 2, 89:11) raised the reasoning that perhaps it was permitted to disguise oneself as a gentile, since there are secular gentiles, and so this does not express acceptance of their religion. (Regarding the Jewish anusim who converted to Christianity under the decrees in Spain, and in their homes tried to preserve their Jewish identity in the hope that the decree would be annulled and they would return to Judaism – there is room to say that once they had already acted not in accordance with halakha, and had transgressed and desecrated God's Name and not been killed, from then on their aim should be to preserve life and to try to escape to another place, even if in the meantime they would have to continue dressing and behaving as Christians. For by being killed there would no longer be Kiddush Hashem, but perhaps the opposite. In addition, by being killed they would cause many others who had considered returning to Judaism to retreat from their intention. And also, by being killed they would not bring about the annulment of the decree, as had already been proven.)

sections.body_en:
Everything we have learned – that under coercion against religion one is obligated to give up one's life rather than transgress – is in order not to commit a transgression. But if one is coerced not to fulfil a positive commandment, for example, not to study Torah, not to put on tefillin or not to affix a mezuza to the doorway – there is no obligation to give up one's life, since by neglecting a mitzva one does not desecrate God's Name through an action. In addition, since they can force him to neglect the mitzva by putting him in prison, he has no way of resisting the neglect of the mitzva. This is not so if he is killed in order not to commit a transgression: then he indeed does not actually commit the transgression.

However, we find that the Sages praised the pious who, in difficult days of government decrees, gave up their lives even for the fulfilment of positive commandments, although they were not obligated to do so. Of them it is stated (Shemot 20:6): "and showing kindness to thousands, to those who love Me and keep My commandments" – "These are Israel, who dwell in the Land of Israel and give their lives for the mitzvot. 'Why are you going out to be killed?' – 'Because I circumcised my son.' 'Why are you going out to be burned?' – 'Because I read from the Torah.' 'Why are you going out to be crucified?' – 'Because I ate matza.'" "'Why are you going out to be burned?' – 'Because I kept Shabbat.' 'Why are you being lashed with the whip?' – 'Because I made a sukka, because I took a lulav, because I put on tefillin, because I attached tekhelet, because I did the will of my Father in Heaven'" (Mekhilta, Yitro; Vayikra Rabba 32:1).8

When a person is coerced into a transgression without performing an action himself, even if it is one of the three severe transgressions – he need not be killed. For example, if they forcibly bend his body down before an idol, or a married woman is raped, or they throw him onto a person in order to kill that person – he need not be killed (Rema 157:1).9

notes_en.en:
Shabbat 49a: "Once the wicked Roman government issued a decree against Israel that whoever put on tefillin would have his brain pierced. Elisha would put them on and go out to the marketplace. A quaestor (Roman official) saw him; he ran from him, and the quaestor ran after him. When he reached him, he (Elisha) removed them from his head and held them in his hand. He said to him: What is that in your hand? He said to him: The wings of a dove. He opened his hand and they were found to be the wings of a dove. Therefore they call him Elisha Ba'al Kenafayim (Elisha, Master of Wings)." From the fact that Elisha removed the tefillin, we learn that even at a time of a decree of persecution there is no obligation to be killed for neglecting a positive commandment. So wrote Ramban, Ran and Ritva there; Nimukei Yosef on Sanhedrin 74b. In addition, there is no possibility of refusing to let the gentile prevent him from fulfilling a mitzva, for if they put him in prison, he will not be able to fulfil the mitzva (Ramban, Shabbat ibid.; Nimukei Yosef and Ran on Sanhedrin and on Shabbat). However, from Rambam (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4) it is implied that one is killed even for positive commandments (Leḥem Mishneh; Mishpat Kohen 144, p. 321, paragraph 2; Einayim La-mishpat). So wrote Rivash 171. But the opinion of most poskim is that there is no obligation to be killed for positive commandments. So wrote Radbaz 4:92; Beit Yosef and Rema 157:1.
And although there is no obligation of self-sacrifice for positive commandments, in practice, when the wicked of the nations issued decrees against Israel, and there was a need to arouse hearts to protest against the attempt to make Israel forget the mitzvot, many gave up their lives for them. So it was at the time of the decrees of Antiochus (I Maccabees 1:52, 61-62; She'iltot, Ḥanukka 27), and so acted Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon, who defied the decree and taught Torah in public. So too it is cited in the Mekhilta and the Midrash quoted above. And so it is clear from the words of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar (Shabbat 130a): "Every mitzva for which Israel gave themselves over to death at the time of a government decree, such as idolatry and circumcision, is still held firmly in their hands; and every mitzva for which Israel did not give themselves over to death at the time of a government decree, such as tefillin, is still weak in their hands.

When a Jew is coerced to commit one of the three severe transgressions passively (shev ve-al ta'aseh), even in public – he need not be killed. This accords with Abaye's statement (Sanhedrin 74b) that Esther did not give up her life because she was like 'karka olam' (the ground of the world), that is, she did not perform the act of transgression herself. And although Rava explained it differently (that it was for their own pleasure), Abaye's words were also accepted as halakha (Rif, Sanhedrin 17b, and Rosh, Ketubot 1:4, as cited in Shakh 157:9; Ḥinukh 296; Ramban, Ran and Nimukei Yosef, Sanhedrin 74b; Responsa Rashba 1:10; Ritva, Shabbat 49a; Rema 157:1). (However, some say that in public, in order to make one transgress his religion, one must be killed rather than transgress even passively. So wrote Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Toldot Adam Ve-Ḥava 18:3, as cited in Gilyon Maharsha on the Shakh ibid.; and some hold that this is the opinion of Rambam: Tosefet Yom Ha-kippurim, Yoma 82a; Mishpat Kohen 144.)

sections.title_en: Is It Permitted to Give Up One's Life When Not Obligated?
sections.body_en:
When there is no need to give up one's life for the fulfilment of the mitzvot, it is forbidden to give up one's life, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:5): "You shall keep My statutes and My laws, which a person shall do and live by them" – "'and live by them' – and not die by them"; from here we learn that saving life overrides all the mitzvot in the Torah (Yoma 85b). Therefore, it is forbidden to refrain from desecrating Shabbat in order to save a dangerously ill person, and a dangerously ill person who needs to eat is forbidden to fast on Yom Kippur. So too with the other mitzvot: it is forbidden to fulfil a mitzva while endangering one's life. Anyone who dies after endangering himself to fulfil a mitzva bears a grave sin, and he is like one who sheds blood, for he is guilty of his own death (see Yerushalmi Yoma 8:5).

Likewise, when a gentile coerces a Jew to commit a transgression for the gentile's own benefit, without any wish to make him transgress his religion, the Jew is forbidden to give up his life. And if he did give up his life, he is liable for his own life. On the other hand, we learned in the previous section that in difficult times, when there was a need to arouse hearts against the decrees of rulers aimed at making Israel forget the mitzvot, the Sages praised those who chose to give up their lives, although they were not obligated to do so.

There are also intermediate situations, in which it is unclear whether the gentile's entire intention is to make him transgress his religion or whether he also intends his own benefit (above, note 4), or there is doubt whether the gentile truly intends to kill the Jew if he does not transgress, or it is unclear whether an act done in private is known to many (above, section 6). In all these intermediate situations, because of the doubt there is no obligation to give up one's life, and if he wishes to be stringent with himself – he may be killed. So the Jerusalem Talmud relates (Sanhedrin 3:5) about Rabbi Abba bar Zemina, who was a tailor and worked for a gentile master in Rome. The gentile master served him nevela (meat of an animal not ritually slaughtered), and he refused to eat. The gentile threatened that if he did not eat, he would kill him. Rabbi Abba replied: 'Even if you kill me, I will not eat.' The gentile said: 'Who told you that I meant to test you? On the contrary, had you eaten, I would have killed you, for a Jew should behave like a Jew and a gentile like a gentile; and now that you did not eat, I will not kill you.' Rabbi Mana said: Had Rabbi Abba acted according to the strict letter of the halakha and eaten, he would have been killed.

That is to say, from the standpoint of halakha, since the coercion was in private, Rabbi Abba should have eaten and not endangered himself. In addition, it is possible that the gentile did not intend to make him transgress his religion but only to abuse him, and then for this reason too he should have eaten. On the other hand, it is possible that Rabbi Abba was in doubt whether the gentile truly intended to carry out his threat, and feared that if he yielded and ate, the gentile would publicise it and cause Ḥillul Hashem, and perhaps even demand that he convert. In any case, from the fact that the Yerushalmi brought this story with its various aspects, we learn that in situations of doubt a person may uphold the principles of his faith and be killed, although he is not obligated to do so (SA 157:1; Shakh 1).

To understand this halakha, it must be explained that although one should strive for clear guidance on every question, and especially on grave questions of life and death, there will inevitably be intermediate situations in which the decision rests with the individual. It is like wartime, when it is impossible to determine in advance how every commander and soldier should act in every situation, since many factors are unknown and situations change and shift: sometimes a charge will lead to victory and sometimes to defeat; sometimes one must use cunning and sometimes a direct and forceful response; sometimes one must outflank from the right and sometimes from the left. Even when in hindsight one can think about what would have been best to do, there is no way of knowing it in advance. And since people conduct war, they will always make mistakes. Therefore, above all the instructions there must be a fundamental principle: without readiness to risk one's life with responsible judgement, there is no chance of victory and defeat is assured, and every commander and soldier must act with courage and responsibility for the sake of victory. Similarly with the mitzva of Kiddush Hashem: the fundamental principle is that every person must sanctify the Name of Heaven – usually by diligently preserving life, in which case it is forbidden to be killed in order to fulfil a mitzva, and if he is killed he desecrates God's Name; and sometimes through self-sacrifice, in which case he must be killed rather than transgress. And there are intermediate situations in which there is no obligation to give up one's life, but there is merit in doing so, and then one who wishes to be stringent with himself in order to sanctify the Name of Heaven – may do so.10

notes_en.en:
According to Tosafot (Avoda Zara 27b, s.v. "Yakhol"), Maharam of Rothenburg and Rosh (Avoda Zara 2:9), when a gentile coerces a Jew to transgress his religion by committing one of the transgressions, even in private and for the gentile's benefit, if he wishes to be stringent with himself and be killed – he may. The source of their words is the Yerushalmi (Sanhedrin 3:5) cited above (and according to Semak 3 and Orḥot Ḥayim, it is even a measure of piety to be killed rather than transgress). On the other hand, according to Rambam (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4), when there is no obligation to give up one's life it is forbidden to do so, and if he gave up his life, he is liable for his own life. So wrote Ramban, Nimukei Yosef and Ḥinukh. Seemingly this is a polar dispute, but when we look more deeply we will see that in practice the opinions are close to one another. First, Rambam himself wrote in Iggeret Ha-shemad (p. 53 in Rav Yitzḥak Shilat's edition) that even when there is no obligation to give up one's life, because the demand is only to declare belief in the prophecy of Muhammad without any commitment to violate the Torah, one who gave up his life "has performed a mitzva and has a great reward before God, may He be exalted, because he gave up his life for the sanctity of God's Name." Yad Peshuta explained that since he mistakenly thought that he was required to give up his life, he has a great reward, but initially he is forbidden to give up his life. Rav Shilat explained that this refers to a special case in which it is permitted to give up one's life but not obligatory, since everyone knows that he says he believes in Muhammad only with his lips. End of quote. In addition, according to Ramban (Shabbat 49a), who follows Rambam's approach, in a time of persecution it is permitted to give up one's life even for positive commandments, although there is no obligation to do so. Perhaps Rambam in Iggeret Ha-shemad should be explained in this direction. Likewise, according to Ḥinukh (296), who follows Rambam's approach, a great, wise and pious person is permitted to give up his life even for positive commandments in order to fortify the generation, as Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon did. And according to Nimukei Yosef (Sanhedrin 18a in the pages of the Rif), any pious person is permitted to do so (according to Mishpat Kohen 144, it is implied that Rambam does not agree with this). On the other hand, regarding the opinion of the Rosh, some restrict the permission to give up one's life to the case where the coercion to commit one of the transgressions is in order to make one transgress his religion, but if it is for the gentile's benefit – it is forbidden. So wrote Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (although according to Maharik 137 and those who agree with him, according to the Rosh one may give up one's life even when the coercion is for the gentile's benefit). Also, since the Rosh did not present his opinion as disputing Rambam, it is implied that in his view there is no great dispute here. It emerges that in practice the dispute is confined to the case of coercion to transgress one's religion not in a time of persecution and in private, and regarding this SA 157:1 ruled that he may give up his life. But when it is a matter of danger to life due to illness and the like, all agree that it is forbidden to give up one's life in order to fulfil a mitzva, for self-sacrifice applies only in a situation of coercion against the mitzva, in which case self-sacrifice involves Kiddush Hashem (Radbaz 4:67).
Second, when we look more deeply, we find that in practice there is almost no situation in which it is clear that the coercion is against religion and in private, so that the law would depend on this dispute. For as explained above, reality is very complex, and sometimes it is impossible to know the gentile's exact intention – whether it is to make one transgress his religion, and whether he will really kill if one does not transgress – and when the coercion is in private, there is sometimes a doubt whether it may become known to many. Therefore, just as in war it is impossible to set clear instructions but only general guidance, as explained above, so it is with self-sacrifice. This also emerges from Terumat Ha-deshen 199, cited in Shakh 157:1, who wrote that seemingly one should be lenient and not give up one's life, in accordance with the principle "in a doubt concerning life, we are lenient"; but on the other hand, we find that with Kiddush Hashem the Sages were not particular about loss of life; therefore he concluded that the ruling depends on the circumstances.

sections.title_en: Self-Sacrifice of the Righteous for the Needs of the Generation
sections.body_en:
When there is a need to fortify the generation and strengthen faith, even in a situation where there is no obligation to give up one's life, great and wise people may give up their lives in order to strengthen the spirit of the public to cleave to God with courage – provided that they examine carefully that their self-sacrifice will indeed strengthen faith and not weaken it (Ḥinukh 296; Nimukei Yosef on the Rif, Sanhedrin 18a; Maharik).

So acted Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya: when they saw that many Jews were bowing to Nevukhadnetzar's statue, they chose to give up their lives and be cast into the fiery furnace rather than bow to it (Daniel 3; Megilla 12a). By law they were not obligated to give up their lives, for this statue was not idolatry but a monument meant to glorify him as king (Rabbeinu Tam), and they could even have fled elsewhere and been spared the need to bow to the monument. But since they saw the breach of the generation – that many were stumbling into idolatry and assimilating among the gentiles – they wanted to give an example and model of self-sacrifice, in order to strengthen the generation to cleave to the faith of Israel. And since in the eyes of the public the statue was perceived as idolatry, or at least as something that diminished the honour of Heaven by demanding obedience to the king and not to God, they chose to stay and not bow and to give up their lives for Kiddush Hashem (Tosafot, Pesaḥim 53b, s.v. "Mah"; Ramban and Rashba, Ketubot 33a). Of that dark period the Sages said (Sanhedrin 93a): "The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to turn the entire world into night… and into blood… but when He looked at Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya, His mind was calmed." For in their merit the people of Israel remembered its covenant with the Lord its God, returned to its land, and built the Holy Temple and the walls of Jerusalem. And for future generations as well, their self-sacrifice served as a model and example for the holy ones of Israel who gave up their lives for the sanctity of God's Name.

So too acted Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon: when the government decreed that Torah not be studied, he stood up, gathered assemblies and taught Torah in public. And although Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma told him that it was not right to endanger himself in this way, he continued on his path until he was killed for Kiddush Hashem (Avoda Zara 18a).

We likewise find (Sanhedrin 14a) that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava gave up his life for the continued transmission of semikha (rabbinic ordination), on which the authority of the judges of the Sanhedrin depends, although there is no obligation to give up one's life for this, since it is a positive commandment. "Once the wicked government decreed persecution upon Israel: whoever ordains will be killed, whoever is ordained will be killed, the city in which they ordain will be destroyed, and the boundaries in which they ordain will be uprooted. What did Yehuda ben Bava do? He went and sat between two great mountains, between two large cities, and between two Shabbat boundaries, between Usha and Shefar'am (so that they could not accuse and punish any city or boundary), and ordained five elders there… When their enemies discovered them, he said to them: My sons, run! They said to him: Rabbi, what will become of you? He said to them: I lie before them like a stone that cannot be overturned. It was said that they did not move from there until they had driven three hundred iron lances (spears) into him and made him like a sieve."

The Sages said (Berakhot 61b): "Once the wicked government decreed that Israel must not engage in Torah study. Pappos ben Yehuda came and found Rabbi Akiva gathering assemblies in public and engaging in Torah. He said to him: Akiva, are you not afraid of the government? He said to him: I will tell you a parable; to what can this be compared? To a fox walking along the bank of a river, who saw fish gathering from place to place. He said to them: Why are you fleeing? They said to him: Because of the nets that people bring against us. He said to them: Would you like to come up onto dry land, and you and I will live together as my ancestors lived with your ancestors? They said to him: Are you the one they call the cleverest of animals? You are not clever but foolish! If in the place where we live we are afraid, in the place where we die, how much more so! So too with us: now, when we sit and engage in Torah, of which it is written (Devarim 30:20): 'For it is your life and the length of your days' – this is how it is; if we go and neglect it – how much more so! It was said that only a few days passed before they seized Rabbi Akiva and imprisoned him, and they seized Pappos ben Yehuda and imprisoned him next to him. He (Rabbi Akiva) said to him: Pappos! Who brought you here? He (Pappos) said to him: Fortunate are you, Rabbi Akiva, who were seized for words of Torah; woe to Pappos, who was seized for idle matters. When they took Rabbi Akiva out to be executed, it was the time for reciting Shema, and they were raking his flesh with iron combs, and he was accepting upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. His students said to him: Our master, even to this point?! He said to them: All my days I was troubled by this verse, 'with all your soul' – even if He takes your soul. I said: When will the opportunity come to me so that I may fulfil it? And now that it has come to me, shall I not fulfil it?! He prolonged the word 'eḥad' (One) until his soul departed with 'eḥad'. A heavenly voice went forth and said: Fortunate are you, Rabbi Akiva, that your soul departed with 'eḥad'… Fortunate are you, Rabbi Akiva, for you are destined for the life of the World to Come."

Pappos was apparently released from that imprisonment, but later Pappos too was sanctified through self-sacrifice. The Sages said (Ta'anit 18b): "When Trajan wished to kill Lulianus and his brother Pappos in Laodicea, he said to them (mockingly): If you are of the people of Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya, let your God come and save you from my hand, just as He saved Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya from the hand of Nevukhadnetzar. They said to him: Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya were completely righteous, and they were worthy of having a miracle performed for them, and Nevukhadnetzar was a proper king, and it was fitting for a miracle to be performed through him. But that wicked man (Trajan) is a commoner, and it is not fitting for a miracle to be performed through him. And we have incurred the penalty of destruction before the Omnipresent, and if you do not kill us, the Omnipresent has many executioners, and the Omnipresent has many bears and lions in His world who could attack us and kill us. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, handed us over to you only so that He will in the future exact our blood from your hand. Nevertheless, he killed them immediately. It was said that they did not move from there until two officers (diyuflei) came from Rome and split his (Trajan's) skull with clubs."

And for what were Lulianus and Pappos seized? Some say that the daughter of the Roman ruler was found murdered, and they decreed upon the Jews of Lod that if they did not hand over the murderer, they would kill them all. Lulianus and Pappos volunteered and said, "We killed her," and they went out to be executed and saved all their brethren (Rashi, Bava Batra 10b). The Sages further related about them (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 3:5) that they were given water in a cup coloured red, so that it would look as though they were drinking gentile wine in violation of the prohibition. But they refused to desecrate the Name of Heaven and to drink it, and for this they were executed (Tosafot, Shabbat 72b, s.v. "Rava"; Ran, Pesaḥim 50a). It is possible that both events happened to them: after they confessed that they had killed the ruler's daughter, they were offered rescue if they would betray their Judaism and drink gentile wine, or at least water in a red cup, and they refused and were killed. And although they were not known as Torah scholars or righteous men, the Sages said (Pesaḥim 50a) of the martyrs of Lod: "No one can stand within the partition of those executed by the government." For they gave up their lives for their national and religious honour and for the rescue of their brethren (in Imrei No'am by the Gra, Berakhot 61b, it is explained that this is the same Pappos; and there are other opinions).

sections.title_en: The Story of the Woman and Her Seven Sons
sections.body_en:
It happened that a woman and her seven sons were brought before the emperor and his servants. They ordered the eldest to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (Shemot 20:2): "I am the Lord your God." They took him out and killed him. They brought the second before the emperor and ordered him to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (ibid.): "You shall have no other gods before Me." They took him out and killed him. They brought the third and ordered him to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (Shemot 22:19): "One who sacrifices to the gods, other than to the Lord alone, shall be destroyed." They took him out and killed him. They brought the fourth and ordered him to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (Shemot 34:14): "You shall not bow down to another god." They took him out and killed him. They brought the fifth and ordered him to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (Devarim 6:4): "Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is One." They took him out and killed him. They brought the sixth and ordered him to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (Devarim 4:39): "Know this day and take it to your heart that the Lord is God in the heavens above and on the earth below; there is no other." They took him out and killed him. They brought the seventh and ordered him to worship idolatry. He said to them: It is written in the Torah (Devarim 26:17-18): "You have affirmed the Lord this day to be your God… and the Lord has affirmed you this day to be His treasured people… We have already sworn to the Holy One, blessed be He, that we will not exchange Him for another god, and He too has sworn to us that He will not exchange us for another nation." The emperor said to him: I will throw down my seal, and you bend down to the ground to pick it up, and in doing so you will appear to be bowing to the idol, so that people will say that you have accepted the king's decree, and in this way you will be saved. The seventh son answered him: "Woe to you, Caesar, woe to you, Caesar! If for your own honour it is so, for the honour of the Holy One, blessed be He, how much more so!" They took him out to kill him. The mother asked: Give him to me so that I may kiss him a little before you kill him. She said: "My sons, go and tell Avraham your father: You bound one altar, and I bound seven altars!" The Sages said: "She too went up to the roof, fell and died. A heavenly voice went forth and said: 'A joyful mother of children'" (Gittin 57b). For all generations, the figures of the mother and her seven sons have remained exemplary figures of self-sacrifice for the faith. In the merit of the holy ones who gave up their lives, our people endures, and in their merit the world continues to advance toward its redemption.

Concerning them the Sages expounded the verses (Tehillim 16:1-5): "Protect me, O God, for I have taken refuge in You. You have said to the Lord: You are my Lord; my good is not incumbent upon You. For the holy ones who are in the land, and the mighty ones in whom is all my delight. Their sorrows shall be multiplied who hasten after another; I will not pour out their libations of blood, nor take their names upon my lips. The Lord is my allotted portion and my cup; You support my lot." David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Why are "their sorrows multiplied"? Why did You multiply the sorrow of the generation of persecution, who were righteous and hastened to come to Your doorway (to the synagogues and study halls) and were late to leave, and were killed for the sanctity of Your Name?! When the wicked among the gentiles would say to one of them: Pour a libation before the idol – he would say: I will not pour a libation. Sacrifice to the idol – and he would say: I will not sacrifice. Drink water, even in a red cup (which looks like libation wine) – and he would say: I will not drink. Make a vow in the name of the idol – and he would say: I will not vow, for so Moshe our teacher commanded me in his Torah. And for this they are killed! The Holy One, blessed be He, answered David: The holy ones have lost nothing, for their blood is more precious before Me than all the sacrifices, and their status is great – "nor take their names upon my lips," for their names may not be uttered without holy awe. They are God's portion and lot – they can say: "The Lord is my allotted portion and my cup; You support my lot." Moreover, the holy ones who were killed for Kiddush Hashem are those who supported Israel at Mount Sinai, for in their merit Israel received the Torah, and in their merit God forgave Israel for the sin of the Golden Calf (based on Shoḥer Tov, Tehillim 16:4-5).11

notes_en.en: My great-grandfather on my mother's side, the Rav and Ga'on Dr. Ḥayim Yehuda Weil, served in the rabbinate for forty years in communities in Germany, Czarnikau and Düsseldorf. His nephew related that when he was a child, while the world was still relatively calm, his uncle, Rav Weil, visited their home. In order to educate them in loyalty to the Torah, he told them about his own great-grandfather (from whom the nephews were the fifth generation), who was murdered in the pogroms in Poland "al kiddush Hashem" (for the sanctification of God's Name). He also told them about Rabbi Akiva, who was killed "al kiddush Hashem." He told the whole story in German, but the words "al kiddush Hashem" he said in the Holy Tongue and with holy awe, and they shook him as a child to the marrow of his bones. Grandfather did not know how far these words would reach. When the Nazi persecutions began, he refused offers to flee, saying that the captain must be the last to leave the ship. After Kristallnacht and the destruction of the community in Düsseldorf, he fled to Holland, where the family of his daughter Flora had fled earlier. When Holland too was occupied, he refused to endanger a Dutch family in order to save himself, adding that perhaps as a rabbi he could help encourage his brethren in the camps. In 5702 (1942) he was taken to a concentration camp. About a year later, when his turn came to be sent to the extermination camp, he took leave of his neighbours "with a great and serious speech." On 20 Marḥeshvan 5704 (1943), at about the age of 77, he was murdered in Auschwitz al kiddush Hashem.

sections.title_en: Self-Sacrifice for the Honour of Israel
sections.body_en:
A great person who is about to fall into the hands of wicked people who will likely abuse and humiliate him may take his own life, and he fulfils the mitzva of Kiddush Hashem. So acted King Shaul: when he saw that the Philistines were about to take him captive, he said to his armour-bearer: "Draw your sword and run me through with it, lest these uncircumcised ones come and run me through and abuse me. But his armour-bearer would not, for he was very afraid; so Shaul took the sword and fell upon it" (I Shmuel 31:4). The Sages said that his act did not involve the prohibition of suicide (Bereishit Rabba 34:13). Moreover, before the battle King Shaul heard from Shmuel the prophet that if he fled or surrendered to the Philistines he would save his life, and if he went out to battle he would be killed together with his sons and would merit to be with him in his place in Gan Eden (Vayikra Rabba 26:7). King Shaul decided to go out to battle and to bequeath to the people a heritage of heroism and Kiddush Hashem: as long as there is a chance, they will fight and not surrender. The Philistines did indeed win and Shaul and his sons were killed, but Israel was not enslaved to them. The Sages said (Vayikra Rabba 26:7) that when Shaul decided to go out to that battle, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to the ministering angels: "See the creature I have created in My world… he goes out to war knowing that he will be killed, takes his sons with him, and rejoices in the attribute of justice that strikes him."

Thus, despite his weaknesses, the image of King Shaul has remained that of a hero who gave up his life for the sanctity of God's Name, as King David lamented over him and over his son Yehonatan: "From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Yehonatan did not turn back, and the sword of Shaul did not return empty. Shaul and Yehonatan, beloved and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not parted; they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions… How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Yehonatan, slain upon your high places… How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!" (II Shmuel 1:22-27). The Sages said that Israel was punished for not eulogising Shaul properly (Yevamot 78b).
