And when they went to bring the bones of Shaul and Yehonatan from their temporary burial place to their permanent burial place, they found "that the worm had not prevailed over them, and of him it is stated (Tehillim 34:21): 'He guards all his bones; not one of them is broken'" (Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer 17).

In contrast, as the destruction of the First Temple approached, King Tzidkiyahu did not act heroically and fell into captivity, and the Babylonians abused him, and the honour of Israel was degraded. As it is stated (II Melakhim 25:5-7): "The army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him. They seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Rivla, and they pronounced judgement upon him. They slaughtered the sons of Tzidkiyahu before his eyes, and they blinded the eyes of Tzidkiyahu, bound him in bronze fetters and brought him to Babylon." The Sages said (Eikha Rabba 1:51): "'For these I weep; my eye, my eye runs down with water' (Eikha 1:16) – for the removal of understanding and the removal of the Shekhina. Is it possible that Tzidkiyahu saw others gouging out his eyes and did not have the sense to dash his head against the wall until his soul departed? Rather, he caused his sons to be killed before him."12

notes_en.en: The Sages learned (Bereishit Rabba 34:13) from the verse "But your blood of your lives I will require" (Bereishit 9:5) that, as a rule, suicide is forbidden; but from the word 'akh' ('but') they learned that a great person like Shaul is permitted to take his own life so that enemies will not humiliate him. However, some say that Shaul acted improperly when he took his own life (Da'at Zekenim, Bereishit 9:5, in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Avraham; Orḥot Ḥayim, Ahavat Hashem Ve-yir'ato 1, cited in Bedek Ha-bayit YD 157), or that it was only because of Shmuel's prophecy, from which he knew that he would die, that he was permitted to take his own life (Yefeh To'ar on Bereishit Rabba 9:5; Shiyarei Knesset Ha-gedola YD 157, Hagahot Beit Yosef 21; Rav Pe'alim 3, YD 21). But according to Ramban (Torat Ha-adam, Sha'ar Ha-sof, the section on the eulogy), Shaul was permitted to take his own life, and therefore there was an obligation to mourn and eulogise him, as the Sages said that Israel was punished for neglecting to eulogise Shaul (Yevamot 78b). So it was ruled in Tur and SA YD 345:3, and by many others. And according to Semak (positive commandment 3) and Rabbeinu Peretz there (7), Shaul's suicide even contained an aspect of Kiddush Hashem; Baḥ 157:1 cites them. Similarly, Yam Shel Shlomo (Bava Kamma 8:59) wrote that Shaul wished to prevent the Ḥillul Hashem of the gentiles abusing the king of Israel. Rav Goren elaborated on this (Torat Ha-shabbat Ve-ha-mo'ed, pp. 391-404), and on this basis wrote that soldiers who are about to be taken captive and know that they will be killed amid humiliation may take their own lives so as not to be degraded. Likewise, a soldier who possesses secrets whose disclosure by the enemy could endanger the security of the state, and who fears that information will be extracted from him before he is killed, should take his own life and not allow himself to be subjected to extortion.

sections.body_en:
Sometimes, when it is clear to a person that they are about to force him to transgress his religion against his will while degrading the Divine image within him, he is permitted to give up his life in order to avoid this. As in the story the Sages related (Gittin 57b) about those taken captive at the destruction of the Second Temple: "It happened that four hundred boys and girls were taken captive for disgrace (for prostitution in a brothel). They sensed for what purpose they were wanted. They said: If we drown in the sea, will we come to the life of the World to Come? The eldest among them expounded for them: 'The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea' (Tehillim 68:23). 'I will bring back from Bashan' – I will bring back from between the teeth of the lion; 'from the depths of the sea' – these are those who drown in the sea. When the girls heard this, they all leapt and fell into the sea. The boys drew a kal va-ḥomer (a fortiori inference) for themselves and said: If these, for whom this is the natural way, [act] so, we, for whom this is not the natural way (homosexual relations), how much more so! They too leapt into the sea. Of them the verse says (Tehillim 44:23): 'For Your sake we are killed all day long; we are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.'"

If one being killed for Kiddush Hashem suffers greatly, and nevertheless does not hasten his death even for a moment – he will be called holy. As is related (Avoda Zara 18a) about Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon: when the government decreed that Torah not be studied, he would gather assemblies in public and expound words of Torah with a Torah scroll resting in his lap. They seized him and sentenced him to death by burning. "They brought him and wrapped him in the Torah scroll, surrounded him with bundles of vine branches and set them on fire. They brought tufts of wool, soaked them in water and placed them over his heart so that his soul would not depart quickly. His daughter said to him: Father, must I see you like this? He said to her: Had I been burned alone, it would have been hard for me; now that I am being burned together with a Torah scroll, He who will avenge the affront to the Torah scroll will avenge the affront to me. His students said to him: Rabbi, what do you see? He said to them: The parchments are burning, and the letters are flying away. (They said to him:) You too, open your mouth so that the fire will enter you (so that he would die quickly and not suffer). He said to them: Better that He who gave it should take it, and that one should not harm oneself. The executioner (kaltzatoneiri) said to him: Rabbi, if I increase the flame and remove the tufts of wool from over your heart (which slow your burning and increase your suffering), will you bring me to the life of the World to Come? He said to him: Yes. Swear to me! He swore to him. Immediately he increased the flame and removed the tufts of wool from over his heart, and his soul departed quickly. He too (the executioner) leapt and fell into the fire" – for he sought to atone for his sins as an executioner. "A heavenly voice went forth and said: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon and the executioner are destined for the life of the World to Come. Rabbi wept and said: There is one who acquires his world in a single hour, and there is one who acquires his world over many years."

However, one must ask: how did the executioner take his own life and merit the World to Come? It is possible that he knew he was about to be executed for having violated their decree by easing the suffering of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon. Moreover, sometimes great sinners are permitted to put themselves to death in repentance, to show how great their remorse is.13

There were cases in which wicked Christians coerced entire communities, under threat of murder, to convert to Christianity. The rabbis disagreed whether it is right to act first and kill the children and take one's own life so that they will not stumble into conversion, or whether one must wait in case the decree is annulled. "It happened that a rabbi slaughtered children in a time of persecution, for he feared they would be made to transgress their religion. Another rabbi was with him, who was angry with him and called him a murderer, but he paid no heed to his words. The rabbi who objected said: If I am right, that rabbi will be killed by a strange death; and so it was… And afterwards the decree was annulled, and had he not slaughtered them, they might have been saved" (Orḥot Ḥayim, part 2, 4:1, laws of love and fear of God). Maharam of Rothenburg wrote (Responsa 273): "For many great men would slaughter their sons and daughters, and Rabbeinu Kalonymus also did so." And one who did so and in the end was saved need not do teshuva for it.

notes_en.en:
See Shevut Ya'akov 2:111, who wrote along these lines; Zera Emet 1:89 disagreed with him. Rabbeinu Peretz wrote (Hagahot Semak 3:7): "Those holy ones who slaughtered themselves because they did not trust themselves to withstand the trial are completely holy"; but one who knows that there is no concern that he will stumble because of the suffering is forbidden to hasten his death. So wrote Tosafot (Avoda Zara 18a, s.v. "Ve-al"), Ritva and Agudah there, and Tosafot Ha-Rosh, Gittin 57b. And according to Yam Shel Shlomo (Bava Kamma 8:59), even when he fears that he may transgress because of the suffering – he should not take his own life.
Some say that one who is coerced to transgress under severe torture that is going to continue for a long time may transgress, for the obligation to be killed applies only when the alternative is death, whereas torture without limit is harder. This is what they learned from Ketubot 33b: "Had they flogged (tortured) Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya, they would have worshipped the statue" (Shita Mekubetzet there, based on Rabbi Eliezer). But many hold that even under severe torture he should suffer and not transgress, and what was said about Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya – that under torture they would have transgressed – is because the statue was not actual idolatry (Ritva and Tosafot Ha-Rosh in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, Ketubot 33b).

sections.body_en:
Rabbi Shlomo Luria wrote (Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma 4:9) that when the government compels the Torah scholars of Israel to tell it words of Torah, and they are unable to evade this, the scholars are forbidden to alter the laws written in the Torah and to say of something forbidden that it is permitted or of something permitted that it is forbidden; and even if their lives are threatened, they must not alter the halakha. For one is obligated to give up one's life for Kiddush Hashem, and if they alter the law they are like those who deny the Torah of Moshe. Therefore, when the Roman government sent two officials to the Sages of Israel, demanding that they teach them the Torah, they taught them the Torah correctly, including a law that discriminates between Jews and gentiles, which, had it become known to the government, could have led to their being punished with death. In practice, thanks to the goodwill of the officials, who did not want to inform on them, they were saved (Bava Kamma 38a).

True, we learned (Megilla 9a) that when the Greek king Talmai (Ptolemy) demanded that seventy elders translate the Torah, they changed the text in several places. But there they did not change the meaning of the words, only the wording, so that people would not arrive at errors and heresy from the plain sense of the verses. Moreover, there the holy spirit assisted them, so that they all arrived at the same understanding, although each one translated separately. But to change the laws of the Torah is forbidden, and one must be killed rather than change them.

It seems that the obligation to be killed rather than change the laws of the Torah applies when there is a concern that following the change an error will take root for generations, because people will think that this is what the authorised Sages of Israel, who represent the Torah, actually ruled. But when it is clear that the change was made under pressure from the government in a situation of danger – it is permitted to change, since it is known that the change was made only with the lips and is not correct according to halakha; and so the Sages of Israel acted under the pressure of censorship.14

notes_en.en: Several Aḥaronim mentioned the words of Maharshal as halakha, among them the Shela and Shiyarei Knesset Ha-gedola, and many mentioned him in their writings without stating whether they accepted his words in practice. Responsa Yad Eliyahu (Lublin) 48 wrote that only where there is a possible danger must one take the risk and not alter the words of Torah, but in certain danger one need not give up one's life, for this is not among the transgressions for which one must be killed rather than transgress. And some did not accept the words of Maharshal (Responsa Rabbi Akiva Yosef, OḤ 49). It seems that Maharshal's words are accepted as halakha when the change is made by the authorised Sages of Israel and there is a reasonable concern that as a result an error will take root in Israel; but when there is no such concern, it is permitted to change as needed. Therefore, the Sages of Israel altered printed texts according to the instructions of the censorship, even in matters that change the law, such as 'oved avoda zara' (idolater) or 'akum' in place of 'goy' (gentile), or 'apikoros' in place of 'min' (heretic). This is because everyone knows that the censorship imposed it, and they preferred to print the books with the changes rather than not print them at all.

sections.body_en:
The prohibition of murder is one of the three transgressions which, because of their severity, a person must be killed rather than commit in every situation. Therefore, if wicked people present a person with two options – either you kill so-and-so or we kill you – he must be killed rather than transgress and kill. It is related that a person came with a question to the Amora Rabba: The lord of the city ordered me to kill so-and-so, and if I do not do so he will kill me; may I kill him in order to save my own life? Rabba answered: Be killed and do not kill, for who says that your blood is redder than his? Perhaps his blood is redder! (Sanhedrin 74a). Even when it seems to a person that his blood is redder than his fellow's, for example, when his fellow is close to death, he must be killed rather than kill. For the prohibition of murder is absolute, and under no circumstances may a person save himself by murder (Mishpat Kohen 143, p. 315).

Even when he is not required to kill a person with his own hands but to cause his death – he must be killed rather than transgress. For example, if they demanded that he hand a person over to criminals or to enemies, or show where he is hiding so that they can kill him – he must be killed rather than hand him over. Likewise, if they demanded that he throw a person before a beast of prey and thereby cause his death – he must be killed rather than throw him. Likewise, if they demanded that he give them a weapon with which to kill a person, and without it they could not kill him – he must be killed rather than hand over the weapon. And likewise, if they demanded that he give false testimony in order to have a person executed – he must be killed rather than give false testimony.15

notes_en.en:
For the abizraihu (ancillary prohibitions) of bloodshed as well, one must be killed rather than transgress. So wrote Razah and Nimukei Yosef on Sanhedrin (17b in the pages of the Rif), Ramban, and Ḥinukh 296. Therefore, it is forbidden to hand a person over to death, as explained above and in the next section. Likewise, one must be killed rather than give a weapon to a murderer (Ritva, Pesaḥim 25a; Radbaz 4:92). Likewise, one must be killed rather than throw a person before a beast of prey (Minḥat Ḥinukh 296:25). The same applies to false testimony (Ḥatam Sofer, Ketubot 19a), and to robbing a poor person when this may cause him to die of hunger (Bava Kamma 119a; Aseh Lekha Rav 9:28-29). See above, at the end of note 4, regarding the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael, when he was lenient to transgress and not be killed.
The Sages said (Sota 10b): "It is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to put his fellow to shame in public." From the words of most poskim it is implied that this warning was said in order to warn of the terrible severity of the prohibition of humiliating others, but it is not a halakhic obligation to give up one's life (Meiri, Berakhot 43b; Ḥinukh 240; Iyun Ya'akov; and so wrote Rav Moshe Khalfon Ha-Kohen, Brit Avot on Avot 3:15. This is also implied by Rambam, Hilkhot De'ot 6:8; Hilkhot Teshuva 3:14). On the other hand, from the words of several poskim it is implied that one must give up one's life so as not to humiliate another in public (Tosafot, Sota 10b, s.v. "Noaḥ"; Sha'arei Teshuva 3:137; Binyan Tziyon 172). And some wrote that there is no obligation, but they permitted giving up one's life so as not to humiliate another in public (Penei Yehoshua, Bava Metzia 59a; Pri Megadim in Teivat Gome, inquiry 5; Divrei Shaul, Yosef Da'at YD 345). It seems their intention is that one must, or may, give up one's life in order to prevent a terrible insult that could change a person's standing to the point that he might take his own life, or fall ill and die of grief; but with an ordinary insult there is no place for this.

sections.title_en: Handing a Person Over to Death
sections.body_en:
If a group of people were required to hand over one of their number to be killed, under threat that if they did not hand over one of them, they would all be killed – they must all be killed and not give them one person to be killed (Tosefta Terumot 7:23). But if the demand is to hand over a specific person to be killed, like Sheva ben Bikhri, and if not they will all be killed – they should hand him over and not be killed (Yerushalmi Terumot 8:4). Sheva ben Bikhri was a scoundrel who incited Israel to rebel against King David, and when Yoav, the commander of the army, waged war against him, he fled to the city of Avel Beit Ma'akha and fortified himself there. Yoav began to besiege the city, intending to destroy it and kill its inhabitants, who had aided the rebellion. When a wise woman from the city saw this, she agreed with Yoav that the head of Sheva ben Bikhri would be thrown to Yoav, and in return Yoav would lift the siege. The people of the city did indeed kill Sheva ben Bikhri and throw his head to Yoav; the siege was lifted and the city was saved (II Shmuel 20:16-22).

According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, even if the person whom the gentiles demand be handed over is not liable to death, since it is on his account that the gentiles have come against the whole group, they may hand him over in order to save themselves. And according to Reish Lakish, only if the one they seek is liable to death, like Sheva ben Bikhri, may they hand him over. But if he is not liable to death, it is forbidden to hand him over and thereby cause his death in order to save their own lives. In practice, the poskim disagree as to whose view is the halakha.16

notes_en.en:
After the Yerushalmi (Terumot 8:4) cites the dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish, it relates the story of Ulla bar Koshev, who fled from the government and hid in Lod near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Roman troops surrounded Lod and threatened that if they did not hand him over, they would destroy Lod and kill its inhabitants. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi went to Ulla bar Koshev and persuaded him to give himself up to the Romans. Until then, Eliyahu the prophet had been accustomed to reveal himself frequently to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and from then on he stopped revealing himself. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi fasted several fasts, and Eliyahu the prophet revealed himself to him and said: Shall I reveal myself to informers?! Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi replied: But did I not act according to the halakha? Eliyahu the prophet replied: But this is not 'the teaching of the pious' (mishnat ḥasidim). Some say that the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, both because the halakha generally follows him and because of the story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: although he did not act according to the teaching of the pious, this is the halakha. So wrote Ran, Meiri and Ritva, and so it seems from Ḥinukh, Semag and Semak. On the other hand, some say that the halakha follows Reish Lakish, for Ulla bar Koshev was liable to death by the government, and only for this reason was it permitted to hand him over; and even so, this is not 'the teaching of the pious'. So wrote Rambam (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:5), Mikhtam, Agudah, Taz 157:7, and Shiyurei Berakha 8. 'Liable to death', such that even according to Reish Lakish it is permitted to hand him over, refers to liability under the laws of the gentiles (Baḥ, Taz, Pri Ḥadash, Minḥat Ḥinukh and many others. But according to Ma'aseh Roke'aḥ and Shemen Ha-mishḥa, the permission is on condition that Torah law would also agree to it, that is, in a situation where the law of the kingdom does not deviate from Torah law).
Seemingly, there is a difficulty with the approach of Reish Lakish: we learned that the reason one may not kill a person in order to be saved is 'what makes you think your blood is redder?'; but if that person will be killed in any event, why not hand him over and save the rest? The answer is that the reasoning of 'what makes you think' is not the cause of the law but an explanation that makes it plausible; the law stems from the fact that the prohibition of murder is absolute, and therefore under no circumstances may a person save himself by murdering his fellow (Mishpat Kohen 143, p. 314). It has also been explained that even when they threaten to kill everyone, it is forbidden to hand over one person, because if they hand him over he will certainly be killed, whereas there is no certainty that they will carry out the threat to kill everyone (Leḥem Mishneh on Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:5).
When gentiles demand one person for killing, and if not they will kill everyone: some permit them to cast lots as to whom to hand over (Tiferet Le-Moshe YD 157). But many forbid it, because it is permitted to use lots only by means of the holy spirit (Ḥadrei De'ah 157; Naḥal Yitzḥak ḤM 87:3). However, one of them may volunteer in order to save his fellows, as the martyrs of Lod did (above, section 12). Meiri wrote that if they demanded that one person be handed over to be killed, and if not they would kill everyone, and there was a tereifa (a person with a fatal injury) there who was expected to die within that year, they should hand him over in order to save the rest (cited as halakha in Shiyarei Knesset Ha-gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 157:36). But to kill him with one's own hands is forbidden (Degel Re'uven; Tzitz Eliezer 9:17).
Responsa Mi-ma'amakim (5:1) wrote that when the Nazis demanded that Jewish leaders give them a list of Jews who would be saved, while the rest would be killed, it was permitted for them to give a list, since the enemy wished to kill all of Israel, and in such a case whatever can be saved must be saved. Furthermore, Rav Dov Ber Kahana in Kovno ruled that the communal leaders must do everything in their power to save as many Jews as possible, even if in doing so they would cooperate with the Nazis in assembling Jews who would apparently be taken to be killed. Rav Yisraeli wrote (Ḥavat Binyamin 93) that when it involves actual handing over, it is forbidden, even if one thinks it is for the sake of saving others. Moreover, with hindsight it became clear that those who agreed to this helped the Nazis murder more.

sections.body_en:
Just as one must be killed rather than transgress the prohibition of murder, so too with the prohibition of forbidden sexual relations, for the Torah equated the prohibition of murder with the prohibition of forbidden relations, as it is stated (Devarim 22:26): "For as when a man rises against his fellow and murders him, so is this matter" (Sanhedrin 74a). That is to say, there is a particular severity in bloodshed and forbidden relations, for they involve grievous harm to another person. Therefore, if a person is required to rape a woman forbidden to him, and if he does not they will kill him – he must be killed rather than transgress. Likewise regarding the prohibition of male homosexual intercourse: if a person is required to rape a man, and if not they will kill him – he must be killed rather than transgress. And even if the other person consents to being murdered or to the forbidden relations – he must be killed rather than transgress, for these prohibitions are so severe that in every case one must be killed rather than transgress. But if a person is required to lie with an animal, and if not they will kill him, then even though bestiality is as severe as forbidden relations, since it involves no harm to another person – he should transgress and not be killed.

A married woman whom a man is raping and threatening to kill if she does not consent to have relations with him should transgress and not be killed, because she herself does not perform an act, and therefore she is not a participant in the prohibition (she is in the category of 'karka olam', see above, section 9). And even if they threatened to kill her if she does not go to a certain place where she will be raped – she should go and not be killed, since her going does not constitute participation in the transgression itself. Likewise, a man who is forced into homosexual intercourse under threat of death if he refuses should transgress and not be killed.17

notes_en.en:
A woman who was threatened that if she did not submit to relations she would be killed – since she is like 'karka olam', that is, she does not perform the forbidden act – should transgress and not be killed (as Abaye said in Sanhedrin 74b). Only if she is required to bring his member into her in the manner of intercourse, since she performs the act – she must be killed rather than transgress (Tosafot, Rosh and Nimukei Yosef there; Razah and Ramban, Pesaḥim 25a). The same law applies if the man was aroused and they want to thrust him into a forbidden relation: he need not be killed, since he does not perform the forbidden act himself (Rema 157:1). For other acts that a woman is required to do in order to satisfy the lust of one who threatens murder, she should transgress and not be killed, for they are not acts of the prohibition of forbidden relations (Ḥadrei De'ah 157:1; Seridei Esh 2:37). Some are stringent (as implied by Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana EH 150; and according to Meiri, even if they coerce her to go to the place of the rape, she must be killed rather than transgress, whereas the other poskim imply that she should go and not be killed). All this is according to what is accepted by the vast majority of poskim, that Abaye's words were accepted as halakha. But some say that according to Rabbeinu Ḥananel and Rambam there is no permission based on the reasoning of 'karka olam'; rather, the permission applies when the gentile has relations with her for his own pleasure (in their view the halakha follows Rava, who disagrees with Abaye), and therefore if they coerce a married woman to be raped in order to make her transgress her religion, she must be killed rather than transgress (Tosefet Yom Ha-kippurim, Yoma 82a; Mishpat Kohen 144, p. 326, paragraph 4). And according to Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, even according to most poskim, who hold that the permission of 'karka olam' exists, in public, in order to make her transgress her religion – she must be killed rather than transgress.
Gilui arayot for which one must be killed rather than transgress is a union involving a Torah prohibition punishable by court-imposed death or karet, in which kiddushin (betrothal) does not take effect. This includes a man with a married woman, incest and male homosexual intercourse. But for prohibitions that are ordinary negative commandments, such as a divorcée with a kohen, one should transgress and not be killed (Ramban, Ran and Nimukei Yosef on Sanhedrin 74b; Rambam, Hilkhot Ishut 1:5; Rabbi Akiva Eger, YD 157:7).
Nidda: Some are stringent and hold that since relations with a nidda are prohibited on pain of karet, and the prohibition is written in the passage of the arayot, one must be killed rather than transgress (Ritva in the name of Ra'ah there; Radbaz 4:2; Beit Shmuel EH 20:1; and Beit Yosef 195:17 was in doubt about this). And many hold that since kiddushin takes effect with a woman who is a nidda, one should transgress and not be killed (Penei Yehoshua, part 2, EH 44; Avnei Nezer YD 461:10; Ḥelkat Yo'av, part 1, YD 29; Torah Lishmah 494).
If a person was threatened that if he did not lie with an animal they would kill him, then even though it is a forbidden relation punishable by stoning, since he does not harm another person – he should transgress and not be killed (Ritva in the name of Ra'ah, Pesaḥim 25a; and Ran is in doubt about this). According to the She'iltot (42), just as the law of the rodef (pursuer), which is learned from this verse, stems from the harm to the woman – so that it is permitted to strike a pursuer who wishes to rape a married woman against her will, but if she consents it is forbidden to strike him – so too with the law of 'be killed rather than transgress': he must be killed only if she does not consent. But the Rishonim wrote that even if the woman consents, because of the severity of the transgression of forbidden relations, he must be killed rather than transgress (Tosafot, Razah, Ramban and Nimukei Yosef). That is, just as when one is coerced to kill a person who wants to be killed, he must be killed rather than kill (Binyan Tziyon 167), so too if a married woman wants him to have relations with her, since according to the Torah the transgression grievously harms her – he must be killed rather than transgress.
The prohibition for a Jew to have relations with a gentile woman by way of harlotry is rabbinic (from the court of the Ḥashmona'im), and its punishment of karet is from the words of the Prophets (divrei kabbala). On the other hand, one who does this in public, in the presence of ten Jews – it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that "zealots may strike him" (Avoda Zara 36b; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 12:1-4). Therefore, if a Jew is coerced to do so in public – he must be killed rather than transgress (Ramban, Ran, Rema EH 16:2). And in private, since zealots are not permitted to strike him, he should transgress and not be killed, even if she is married (Orḥot Ḥayim, Rivash 171, Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana EH 150, and others. However, according to Nimukei Yosef, if she is married he must be killed rather than transgress).
The prohibition for an unmarried Jewish woman to have relations with a gentile is rabbinic (from the study house of Shem), and her marriage to a gentile is forbidden by Torah law (Avoda Zara 36b; SA EH 16:1). However, she should not be killed over this, since it is a negative commandment that does not carry the death penalty. And if she is married, some say that if she is ordered to transgress actively by bringing his member into her, she must be killed rather than transgress (Rivam; Taz and Shakh 157:14). And some say she should transgress and not be killed, since relations with a gentile are not as significant and severe as full-fledged gilui arayot, for they carry no punishment of death or karet (Rabbeinu Tam, Razah and Ramban).

sections.body_en:
"Women to whom idolaters said: Give us one of you and we will defile her (through harlotry), and if not, we will defile all of you – let them defile all of them, but they must not hand over to them a single soul of Israel" (Mishna Terumot 8:12). For one life is not set aside for another, that is, one is not sacrificed to save others. Even if all of them are married and one is unmarried, they must not hand over the unmarried one (Knesset Ha-gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 157:28).

If one of them was engaged in harlotry, they should hand her over, since the harm to her is not as severe as the harm to the other women (Meiri). But they must not hand over a woman who is not engaged in harlotry, even if she sinned and was promiscuous several times, because rape will harm her more. In addition, perhaps she has had thoughts of repentance, in which case the harm to her would be much more severe (Rashba; Kesef Mishneh, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:5).18

The Sages said (Sanhedrin 75a): "It happened that a certain man set his eyes on a certain woman, and his heart became sick with desire. They came and asked the physicians, who said: He has no remedy unless she has relations with him. The Sages said: Let him die, and she shall not have relations with him. [The physicians then said: He has no remedy unless] she stands before him naked. [The Sages said:] Let him die, and she shall not stand before him naked. [The physicians then said: He has no remedy unless] she converses with him [in words of desire] from behind a fence. [The Sages said:] Let him die, and she shall not converse with him from behind a fence." Some say that this woman was unmarried, but she wanted no connection with him; and although according to the physicians that man was about to die from this, the Sages did not ask her to respond to him even with a conversation in words of desire as the physicians had instructed, "because of the blemish to the family," or "so that the daughters of Israel should not be unrestrained in sexual matters."19

At a time of danger to the whole of Israel, in order to save them, it is permitted to submit to forbidden relations, as Yael and Queen Esther did.20

notes_en.en:
However, according to Dagul Mi-revava (157:1) and Avnei Nezer (YD 129:10-13), if one of them has already been raped, they should hand her over, because the harm to her is less severe.
If the gentiles demanded a specific woman, some say this law is like the law of handing someone over to be killed: according to the poskim who follow Rabbi Yoḥanan (above, section 18), they should hand her over and not all be defiled (Ran). And according to the poskim who follow Reish Lakish, they must not hand her over. However, even according to their approach, if they threatened that if they did not hand her over they would kill all the women, they should hand her over and not all be killed. For in handing her over there is no severe sin of forbidden relations, since the woman who is raped is in the category of 'karka olam' and is not a participant in the sin (Taz 157:9).
Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana (YD 74) wrote that a community required by the government to hand over youths to the army may not choose frivolous and unrestrained youths, since military service involves mortal danger, and one may not sentence them to death for their frivolity. Furthermore, their sin has not been established by testimony. Furthermore, perhaps it is merely youthful wildness. Imrei Esh (YD 52) wrote that it is permitted to pay money to someone who is willing to be handed over to the army in place of another person.

The story is expanded in She'iltot 42: "Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: It happened that a certain man, whose name was Natan ben Tzutzita, set his eyes on a certain woman, a married woman named Ḥanna, and set his heart on defiling her. He sent her gold and silver to lie with her, but she did not accept, and from the intensity of his desire he fell ill and was sick for many days…". The Ḥida, in Petaḥ Einayim, wrote that he is the man about whom Rashi wrote (Sanhedrin 31b, s.v. "Le-dazyo"): "And I found in a book of aggada that Mar Ukva was a penitent, who set his eyes on a certain woman, and his heart became sick with desire and he fell ill. She was a married woman. Some time later she needed to borrow from him, and out of her distress she consented to him; but he conquered his inclination and sent her away in peace, and he was healed. When he would go out to the marketplace, a candle would burn over his head from Heaven, and for this reason he is called Rabbi Natan Tzutzita in tractate Shabbat (56b)." From this we learn that at first the woman did not want him. According to the aggada that Rashi cited, the woman was married, but in the Gemara, Sanhedrin 75a, an opinion is also cited that the woman was unmarried, and nevertheless the Sages ruled stringently for the reasons cited above.
Many explain that the Sages did not take the man's danger into account, since he brought it upon himself by his decision to lust after her (Tosafot of the Sages of England, Sanhedrin 75a; Radbaz 4:2; Ya'avetz, Migdal Oz 1:11-14; Shem Aryeh EH 33; Sefat Emet, Pesaḥim 25a; and others). It is also possible that the Sages held that the physicians exaggerated his danger, as is evident from the fact that at first they said he had no remedy unless she had relations with him, and afterwards they changed their position (Ya'avetz ibid., and others).
Rambam did not write that one must be killed for the abizraihu of forbidden relations, but only for actual forbidden relations (Minḥat Ḥinukh 296:19). But many hold that just as with bloodshed one is killed even for its abizraihu (above, note 15), so too for the 'abizraihu of arayot' one must be killed rather than transgress; that is, for all the forbidden relations for which one must be killed rather than transgress (above, note 17), one must also be killed for the Torah prohibition of touching with desire without intercourse (Ran, Meiri, Maharam Ḥalawa, Orḥot Ḥayim, Shakh 157:10; Beit Shmuel EH 20:1; Ḥavot Ya'ir 182). And some say that one must be killed rather than transgress even their rabbinic prohibitions (Rivash 255; Responsa Re'em 1:59). It seems that those who hold that one must be killed for the 'abizraihu of arayot' are referring to a situation from which there is a high likelihood of reaching actual forbidden relations, similar to the cases of the abizraihu of bloodshed that cause the death of another person. (See Igrot Moshe EH 1:56.)

Yael, the wife of Ḥever the Kenite, seduced Sisera, the army commander who fought against Israel, to lie with her in order to exhaust him, kill him and save Israel. Of her Devora the prophetess said in her song (Shofetim 5:24-27): "Blessed above women be Yael, the wife of Ḥever the Kenite; above women in the tent shall she be blessed…". The Sages said of Yael (Nazir 23b): "A transgression for the sake of Heaven is greater than a mitzva not for the sake of Heaven." So wrote Tosafot (Yevamot 103a, s.v. "Ve-ha"; Sanhedrin 74b, s.v. "Esther") and Maharik 167. According to Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana (YD 161), the mitzva applies specifically to saving the whole of Israel, but there is no permission to save a community. So wrote Maran Ha-rav Kook (Mishpat Kohen 143, p. 309). Some permitted it also for the needs of the many; so wrote Meiri, Sanhedrin 74b; Shevut Ya'akov 2:117. Similarly, after Mordekhai asked Esther to plead for her people, Esther went to Aḥashverosh to appease him so that he would heed her and annul the decree of extermination against the people of Israel. Some say that Esther was a married woman (Megilla 15a), and then from her too one can learn that in order to save Israel she was permitted to submit to forbidden relations, and she bears no blemish from this; on the contrary, she merited prophecy and was counted among the seven prophetesses of Israel (ibid. 14a), and her story was included in the Writings (ibid. 7a).

sections.title_en: One Who Should Have Been Killed but Was Not
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, for the three severe transgressions one must be killed rather than transgress in every situation. However, if he transgressed and was not killed, although he desecrated God's Name, he does not receive lashes, and all the more so he is not liable to death, since he transgressed under duress. Even if he killed a person because he was coerced, he is not punished with the punishment set for this sin in the Torah (although the court may punish him as a temporary measure, hora'at sha'a).

Similarly, Jews who converted to another religion under duress and then repented are not disqualified from giving testimony (Responsa Rosh 54:1; SA and Rema EH 17:6). For only a transgression for which one is punished by the court disqualifies a person from testimony, and one who transgresses under duress is not punished (Noda Bi-Yehuda Kamma EH 72).21

notes_en.en:
In Sifra (Kedoshim 4:8) and Sifrei (Shofetim 149) it is explained that one who worships idolatry under duress or by mistake is exempt from the death penalty. So wrote Rambam (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4): although one is obligated to be killed rather than commit the three severe transgressions, if he transgressed and was not killed, he desecrated God's Name but is exempt from punishment, "for lashes and death are imposed only on one who transgresses willingly, with witnesses and a warning." This is the opinion of most Rishonim (Ramban and Ritva, Avoda Zara 54a; Responsa Rashba 7:41; Ḥinukh 295; Ran, Sanhedrin 64a; Rivash 4), and so wrote Rema 157:2. On the other hand, some hold that if he was warned, even if he transgressed under duress he is liable to death (Hagahot Ramakh, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4, regarding idolatry; Rabbeinu David, cited in Ḥiddushei Ha-Ran, Sanhedrin 61b, regarding the three severe transgressions. This also emerges from Yere'im 270 and Hagahot Maimoniyot, Avoda Zara 3:2).
However, when it is forbidden to be healed through idolatry even when life is at stake (above, section 4), and one transgressed and was healed, the court punishes him with "the punishment fitting for him" (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:6). This implies that the punishment is rabbinic (Divrei Yirmiyahu; Rav Kafiḥ). And some hold that he is punished by Torah law, since in practice the act of being healed was done willingly and not under duress (Or Same'aḥ; Sho'el U-meshiv Tinyana 4:4; Mishpat Kohen 144, p. 332, paragraph 11; Yad Peshuta). Furthermore, he is not considered to be acting under duress, since there is no certainty that he would die from the illness (Ma'aseh Roke'aḥ), and there is also no certainty that the forbidden remedy would save him (Pri Ḥadash).
